questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A research question the design can answer
questions.learningObjective: match a research question to the evidence the design will produce
questions.stem: A team has one reading score per pupil for a single year, no comparison group and no earlier cohort. Which research question can that dataset actually answer?

options.text: How much of the variation in this year's reading scores goes with the hours of reading recorded in the same year?
Does reading more each day cause higher reading scores among this year's pupils?
options.misconception: asks for a cause that a single observational cohort cannot deliver

options.text: How many of this year's pupils read for more than twenty hours a week?
options.misconception: asks for a bare count, which is a fact rather than a question about a relationship

options.text: Will reading scores rise next year if the reading programme is extended?
options.misconception: asks about a future the one-year data set never observes

questions.explanation: The dataset holds two measurements per pupil taken in the same year, so it can describe how strongly they travel together and nothing about what would follow from changing one, and option A is the question that fits. Option B and option D both ask what would happen under a change nobody made and nobody will observe, and a single cohort with no comparison is the design least able to speak to either. Option C is answerable and is simply not a research question, since a count settles itself without any relationship to test.
questions.hint: Ask what the file contains about each pupil, and then refuse any question it cannot reach.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A hypothesis written so it can fail
questions.learningObjective: revise a vague hypothesis into one a result could contradict
questions.stem: A draft states its hypothesis as the mentoring scheme is beneficial for students. Which replacement is written so that a result could count against it?

options.text: Students assigned to the mentoring scheme will show higher mean attainment than students not assigned to it
The mentoring scheme is beneficial for students
options.misconception: leaves beneficial without a quantity or a comparison, so no outcome can fail to support it

options.text: The mentoring scheme is a popular and worthwhile addition to the department
options.misconception: mixes a preference and a value judgement that no data could contradict

options.text: Mentoring will work for most of the students who are assigned to it
options.misconception: adds a word about most without defining the share that would settle the claim

questions.explanation: Falsifiability is a property of the wording: a hypothesis is falsifiable when there is some outcome a reader can point at and say the claim has now failed, and option A supplies an outcome, a comparison and a direction, so a lower mean for the mentored group would count against it. Option B is the sentence it replaces and it can absorb any finding. Option C states a preference and an evaluation, which data may inform without ever refuting. Option D is the subtlest failure, because most appears to be a quantity while leaving unstated how many students the word is meant to cover.
questions.hint: Ask which result would make the sentence untrue.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A rationale that links the gap to the question
questions.learningObjective: identify a rationale whose stated gap actually produces the question
questions.stem: An introduction must justify a proposed study in two sentences. Which pair of sentences makes the link between what is missing and what will be done?

options.text: Prior work compares teaching methods across separate classes but never within one mixed-ability class, so this study asks whether within-class grouping changes reading scores
Prior work has studied reading a great deal, which matters a lot, and this study therefore also studies reading
options.misconception: uses the size of the existing literature as the reason for repeating its question

options.text: Prior work was all carried out elsewhere, so this study carries out the same work closer to home
options.misconception: grounds the study in where prior work happened rather than in what it left open

options.text: Prior work used small samples, so this study uses a large one on the same topic
options.misconception: grounds the study in a methodological complaint that names no open question

questions.explanation: A rationale earns its place by naming a specific absence in prior work and then producing a question that absence generates, and option A does both, because comparing methods within a class is exactly the question the stated gap opens up. Option B treats an abundance of research as a justification for more of it, which is an argument about nothing. Option C confuses where work was done with what it established. Option D is the most common form, since a complaint about sample size is real and can apply to a dozen studies, and it never arrives at a question that only this study can answer.
questions.hint: Ask whether the stated gap contains the question that follows it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A literature review that compares rather than lists
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a synthesising review from a sequence of summaries
questions.stem: A review summarises twenty studies in order of publication, two sentences each. Which change is what turns that into synthesis?

options.text: Group the studies by the point they disagree about and weigh their evidence, so the reader learns what is contested
Cut each summary to a single sentence, so the review fits inside the page limit
options.misconception: shortens the list without creating any relation between its entries

options.text: Order the studies by date rather than alphabetically, so the reader can follow the chronology
options.misconception: rearranges a list without asking any of the studies to relate to another

options.text: Add a closing sentence declaring the field extensive, so the resulting gap looks deliberate
options.misconception: asserts the state of the field rather than demonstrating it from the evidence

questions.explanation: Synthesis is what the review adds by putting studies in relation to one another, and grouping by disagreement forces the writer to say who found what and why the findings cannot all be true, which is the raw material for a research gap. Option B reduces the word count and leaves twenty unconnected entries. Option C supplies a chronology, which is a useful frame for a history of a field and tells a reader nothing about the current disagreement. Option D is the assertion that substitutes for the demonstration, and a reader who has just read twenty unconnected summaries has no way to check the claim.
questions.hint: Ask what the review says that none of the individual studies said.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A search strategy and the selection it produced
questions.learningObjective: identify what a search description must contain for a review to be repeatable
questions.stem: A review reports that searching three databases returned 4,800 records, that 260 were included, and gives nothing else about how the choice was made. Which statement is the fair criticism?

options.text: Without the search strings, dates and exclusion rules, a reader cannot separate the records rightly excluded from the ones missed
The yield is too small for a thorough review, so the search must have been run too narrowly
options.misconception: judges the number of records rather than whether the choice can be repeated

options.text: Two hundred and sixty is too many for a focused question, so the criteria must have been applied loosely
options.misconception: infers criterion strictness from a count of included studies

options.text: Three databases is below the number a complete review requires, so the search cannot be considered thorough
options.misconception: substitutes a fixed count of sources for a description of what was searched

questions.explanation: A review is a study, and a study has to be repeatable, so the description has to let somebody else run the same search, see which records appeared and understand why 4,540 of them were set aside. Without the strings and the rules, the huge majority of the evidence was handled invisibly, and a reader cannot tell a careful exclusion from a mistake. Options B, C and D each measure something countable, and none of those counts carries the information the reader needs, which is why a review can pass all three and still be unrepeatable.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would have to know in order to run the search again.

questions.topic: Citing a primary and a secondary source
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a finding attributable to a source read from one heard about
questions.stem: A paper claims that a trial published in 1998 found no effect of an intervention. The writer has read that finding described in a 2011 review and has not consulted the 1998 report. Which statement describes the citation problem?

options.text: The claim is attributed to a source the writer has not read, and the original report is the place where the finding, its measures and its limits can be checked
The citation is sound, because a review's account of a trial can stand in for the trial itself
options.misconception: assumes a secondary account inherits the primary's authority

options.text: The citation is sound, because the review is the more recent and better-sourced account of the finding
options.misconception: prefers recency over proximity to the original evidence

options.text: The only defect is the missing page number, which the review would have supplied on request
options.misconception: reduces the problem to a formatting requirement

questions.explanation: Attributing a specific finding to a paper means being answerable for what that paper says, and a review that reports a result summarises it in the review's own terms, choosing which details to carry across, so the primary report is where the measure, the sample and the stated limits live. Option B and option C both accept a substitute for a source that was never consulted, and option C makes recency the test, which would rate a passing mention above the original study. Option D reduces a question of attribution to punctuation.
questions.hint: Ask which source could answer a follow-up question about the measure that was used.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A claim cited to an unrelated study
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a citation that cannot support the sentence it is attached to
questions.stem: A sentence says that prior work shows feedback reduces error rates in radiology reporting, and the reference given is a study of colour naming in a map-reading experiment. Which statement is the diagnosis?

options.text: The source does not bear on the claim, so the sentence asserts support that the citation cannot provide until a relevant study is found or the claim is withdrawn
The citation is properly formed, so the only remedy is to soften the wording of the claim
options.misconception: treats a formatting check as though it settled whether the source is relevant

options.text: The citation is acceptable provided a review that mentions both is also listed
options.misconception: believes a bridging reference can carry a claim that no source in it makes

options.text: The claim should be rewritten to match the map-reading study, so that the text and the reference agree
options.misconception: bends the claim to fit an unrelated source instead of checking the source

questions.explanation: A citation is a claim that a particular source supports a particular sentence, and here the source studies a different population, a different task and a different outcome, so the sentence is carrying weight the reference cannot bear. Two honest repairs exist, find a source that bears on the claim, or remove the claim, and both put the text and the evidence back in step. Option B reads relevance as a matter of style, option C invents a broker that does not exist, and option D keeps a citation by rewriting the finding around whatever the cited paper happens to say.
questions.hint: Ask what the cited study measured, and whether it is the thing the sentence is about.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A correlation stated as a cause
questions.learningObjective: identify the verb that asserts an intervention the design never performed
questions.stem: A cross-sectional survey of 1,200 adults records walking hours and a wellbeing score once each. The results sentence says each additional hour of walking increased wellbeing by 0.4 points. Which statement is the accurate objection?

options.text: Nobody's walking was changed, so increased asserts an intervention that did not happen and the figure describes two measurements taken side by side
The sample is too small for the estimate quoted, so the sentence overstates the precision
options.misconception: attacks precision on a claim whose defect is that it has no design behind it

options.text: The wellbeing scale has not been validated, which a survey design cannot repair
options.misconception: raises a separate measurement problem as though it were the causal one

options.text: There is nothing wrong, because a cross-sectional survey is an accepted design for estimating effects
options.misconception: confuses a design being widely used with it supporting the verb used

questions.explanation: Increased describes what happens to people when something is done to them, and in a survey that crosses two measurements taken at one moment nothing was done to anybody, so the only thing the 0.4 can be is the size of the association between two numbers that happen to be in the same records. Option B is worth checking and is a different problem, because the interval around a well-measured association can be perfectly tight while the causal claim still fails. Option C is a genuine limitation that could be stated separately, and option D is the belief that a design inherits permission from its own popularity.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything was done to anyone, and who decided how much.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Where an observational design takes its groups from
questions.learningObjective: name the step an observational comparison cannot take
questions.stem: In a hospital cohort study, nurses recorded whether patients had been given a discharge checklist, and patients reported whether they had used it. The paper says the checklist reduced readmissions. Which statement identifies the design-level problem?

options.text: Receipt and use were recorded rather than assigned, so the groups differ in ways the design cannot balance and the reduction joins giving the checklist to complying with it
Adherence was self-reported, which an administrative record would fix and which is the reason the finding fails
options.misconception: identifies a measurement weakness while ignoring the absence of assignment

options.text: A cohort design cannot measure readmissions accurately over time, so the outcome is the part in doubt
options.misconception: disparages a design's measurement ability rather than its causal limits

options.text: There is no problem, because every eligible patient was offered the checklist
options.misconception: treats universal availability as though it were random assignment

questions.explanation: The groups in this design are made by what happened rather than by what was decided, and patients who comply with a checklist are plausibly different from those who do not in ways that also affect readmissions, so the comparison joins two things and the paper reports one. Option B is a real weakness worth reporting and it is not the reason the causal claim fails, because an administrative record would make compliance more accurate without making it assigned. Option C misplaces the doubt, since cohort designs are routinely used to count readmissions. Option D is the conflation of offered with assigned, which is the step that does the damage.
questions.hint: Ask who decided who was in which group.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What makes an event count interpretable
questions.learningObjective: name the denominator a bare count leaves out
questions.stem: A results section reports that 47 patients had a fall. Which piece of information turns that figure into something a reader can interpret?

options.text: The number of patients who were at risk of falling over the same period, since a count of events carries no rate without its base
The length of the follow-up period, since counts per period and counts per patient are different quantities
options.misconception: supplies a genuine dimension while leaving the denominator still missing

options.text: The severity of each fall, because an unweighted count treats a graver fall like a graver one
options.misconception: adds detail about the events that still does not say how many were at risk

options.text: The number of falls in the comparison ward, because a count is meaningful only beside a comparison
options.misconception: confuses a missing denominator with a missing comparator

questions.explanation: Forty-seven is a number of events and carries no information about how many people were exposed to the risk of falling, so a ward treating forty patients for a week and a ward treating four thousand could both produce it, and only one of those is a problem. Option B fixes a real ambiguity about person-time, and a reader still cannot convert the count into a rate without the denominator. Option C is worth adding to a report and does not repair the omission, and option D addresses a different defect, since a comparison answers whether the count is unusual rather than how large it is.
questions.hint: Ask how many people were in a position to have the event at all.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a percentage multiplies
questions.learningObjective: identify the base a reported percentage leaves unstated
questions.stem: An evaluation states that the scheme improved adherence by 25 per cent. Which information does the reader need in order to turn that sentence into a number of people?

options.text: The quantity the 25 per cent multiplies, since a relative change of that size applied to four events and applied to four hundred describe different numbers of people
The interval around the change, since a percentage without one cannot be called a change at all
options.misconception: supplies precision rather than the missing base

options.text: Nothing further, because the percentage already contains both the before and the after figures
options.misconception: denies that a multiplier can be reversed without the original counts

options.text: The year in which the two figures were taken, since a percentage carries no time reference whatever
options.misconception: asks for dating rather than the arithmetic the percentage depends on

questions.explanation: A percentage is a multiplier and multipliers do nothing until they are applied to something, so the same sentence describes four extra people and four hundred, and the reader cannot tell which the writer meant. Option B is worth reporting and answers a different question, because an interval says how precisely the multiplier is known rather than what it multiplies. Option C is the belief that a rate carries its own denominator, which it does not, and option D asks for a date when the missing item is arithmetic.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer multiplied the twenty-five per cent by.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Reconciling a relative change with a percentage-point change
questions.learningObjective: convert a percentage-point change into the relative change a report quotes
questions.stem: An evaluation reports that compliance rose from 40 per 100 to 50 per 100 and describes the improvement in its headline as 25 per cent. Express that improvement as a relative change, giving the value as a proportion to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The table shows a rise of ten events per hundred while the headline says 25 per cent, and the two can only be reconciled by dividing the rise of ten by the starting value of forty, which gives 0.25. The base is the whole point, because the same ten per hundred would be 20 per cent on a starting value of fifty and a quarter of that on a starting value of forty. Reading the ten as the answer would mistake a change in percentage points for a relative change, which is the error that makes a small movement in a small base look like a large one.
questions.hint: A relative change divides the difference by the value the change started from.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Recovering a denominator from a reported share
questions.learningObjective: invert a reported share to recover the total it was calculated on
questions.stem: A report states that students were 62 per cent of respondents, and separately records 950 non-student respondents, without ever giving a total. Recover the total number of respondents the report implies. Give the value as a whole number.
questions.explanation: If students are 62 per cent then non-students are the remaining 38 per cent, and 950 non-students divided by 0.38 gives 2,500 respondents, of whom 1,550 are students. The two routes agree, since 950 multiplied by the ratio of 0.62 to 0.38 gives 1,550 and adding the non-students returns the same total. A student who divides 950 by 0.62 gets 1,532, which is a plausible-looking total and rests on applying the student share to the non-student count, which is the mismatch that makes the arithmetic feel reasonable while being wrong.
questions.hint: The non-student count is the complement of the stated share, so use that share instead.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Restating an event count as a rate
questions.learningObjective: convert a count and its base into a rate per thousand
questions.stem: A theatre reports 12 unplanned readmissions within 30 days across 4,200 procedures performed in the year. Restate the figure as a rate per 1,000 procedures, giving the value to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Dividing 12 by 4,200 gives 0.002857 readmissions per procedure, and multiplying by 1,000 to change the scale gives 2.857 per 1,000, which is the form that lets a reader compare this theatre with one of a different size. The same result comes from 12 divided by 4.2, since the thousands cancel. Dividing by 1,000 to get 0.012 would leave the figure in the wrong unit, and reporting twelve alone tells a reader that the number is small without telling them how rare it is.
questions.hint: Divide to get a proportion per procedure, then multiply by one thousand.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The row total a percentage column depends on
questions.learningObjective: recover a missing table total from the counts and shares beside it
questions.stem: A results table lists three bands with counts of 48, 72 and 80 and shares of 24, 36 and 40 per cent, but the table gives no total row. Recover the total the shares were calculated on. Give the value as a whole number.
questions.explanation: The three counts add to 200, and the shares confirm it, since 48 over 200 is 24 per cent, 72 over 200 is 36 per cent and 80 over 200 is 40 per cent. The total is what makes the table checkable, because without it any count could be attached to any share and a reader has nothing to verify the percentages against. Dividing the first count by its share gives the same answer, and the reason a total row matters is that this check is the only way a reader can see whether the shares were computed from these counts at all.
questions.hint: Add the counts, and confirm it by dividing one count by its share.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The interval around a reported effect size
questions.learningObjective: compute the lower bound of a standardised effect from its standard error
questions.stem: A report gives a standardised mean difference of 0.40 with a standard error of 0.12 and asks for an approximate 95 per cent interval by adding and subtracting 1.96 standard errors. Compute the lower bound of that interval to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Multiplying 0.12 by 1.96 gives 0.2352, and subtracting that from 0.40 leaves 0.165 as the lower bound, with 0.635 as the upper. The report gives a point estimate on its own, which is the defect the exercise exposes, because a reader cannot tell whether a standardised difference of 0.40 is a reasonably precise finding or one that could plausibly be near zero. Doubling the standard error instead of multiplying by 1.96 gives 0.16, a plausible-looking figure that belongs to a 95 per cent interval only under an assumption that is false here.
questions.hint: Multiply the standard error by the stated multiplier before subtracting.

questions.topic: A table that cannot show whether groups were comparable
questions.learningObjective: identify the column whose absence blocks a comparability claim
questions.stem: A trial reports outcomes separately for the two arms and states that the arms were comparable at baseline, but the table shows only the outcome means and their intervals, with no per-arm counts, ages or baseline scores. Which statement is the accurate objection?

options.text: The comparability claim cannot be checked, because the quantities it rests on are the very ones the table leaves out, so the reader must take it on trust
The claim is well supported, because equal outcome means at baseline are themselves evidence that the arms were comparable
options.misconception: uses the outcome comparison to vouch for a claim about who was in the arms

options.text: Only the intervals are missing, because baseline comparability is a matter for the text rather than for the table
options.misconception: locates a reporting gap in the wrong place, since the values are what is absent

options.text: The objection is answered by the fact that assignment was random, since randomisation alone settles every comparability question
options.misconception: treats randomisation as a substitute for reporting what actually happened

Option B inverts the logic, since similar outcomes say nothing about similar starting points. Option C misplaces the gap, since the text cannot substitute for values that were never reported. Option D is the strongest temptation, because randomisation does make imbalances unlikely, and it still does not license a claim that the realised arms were alike.

questions.topic: An axis that starts away from zero
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a figure whose truncated axis magnifies a small change
questions.stem: A bar chart compares two means of 90.0 and 92.0 units, and the vertical axis is drawn from 88 to 92, so the second bar fills the top half of the plot. Which statement is the fair description?

options.text: The gap occupies half the plotted height while being about two per cent of the values, so the picture magnifies a small difference by a large factor
The chart is sound, because a bar chart is read against its axis rather than against the full possible range of the measure
options.misconception: treats the drawn range as if it settled the question of proportionality

options.text: The chart misleads only if the two bars are drawn in different colours, since the axis range is a matter of presentation
options.misconception: replaces the scale problem with a styling problem

Option D makes disclosure a substitute for design, and a caption in small print below the figure competes against a picture that is already in front of the reader.

questions.topic: A limitations paragraph that names nothing
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a specific limitation from a formulaic caution
questions.stem: A paper's limitations paragraph reads that the study was conducted in a single institution, the sample was relatively small, and further research is needed in larger and more diverse settings. Which statement is the fairest assessment?

options.text: The paragraph names settings rather than the specific way a setting could have produced the result, so it leaves the reader unable to judge how far the finding travels
The paragraph is complete, because it names three limitations and a direction for future work

options.text: The paragraph is too harsh, because single institutions and small samples are ordinary features of published work
options.misconception: defends the study by normalising the very features that should be examined

options.text: The paragraph is weak only because it lacks numbers, since quantified limitations are the only acceptable form
options.misconception: demands a figure for a caution where the missing item is a specific threat

Option B mistakes a list for coverage. Option C is the defensive reflex that treats candour as weakness. questions.topic: A future research suggestion that cannot be settled
questions.learningObjective: recognise a future direction that no design could resolve
questions.stem: A paper closes by saying that the relationship between workload and turnover should be examined further, and that more research is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn. Which statement is the accurate criticism?

The sentence is appropriately cautious, since admitting that a question is open is a fair description of the state of the field

options.text: The sentence is weak only because it fails to promise that the authors will run the next study themselves
options.misconception: makes continuity of personnel the criterion for a research direction

options.text: The sentence would be stronger if it named the direction of the relationship it expects to find

Option C confuses who does the work with whether the question can be settled. Option D asks for a direction, and a stated expectation would narrow what counts as a failure without supplying the design that could produce one.

questions.topic: The share of a truncated axis a gap occupies
questions.learningObjective: compute how much of a plotted axis a difference fills
questions.stem: A figure's vertical axis runs from 88 to 92 units. Two bars stand at 90.0 and 92.0. Compute the share of the plotted axis height that the gap between the bars occupies, giving the value as a proportion to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The axis is four units tall and the gap between the bars is two units, so two divided by four gives 0.50, and that is the proportion of the picture the reader sees as a change. The same two units are a relative change of two over 90, which is 0.0222, so the drawing magnifies the real difference twenty-two and a half times, and a reader glancing at the figure sees half the picture changed when the underlying quantity moved by one part in forty-five. Dividing the gap by the axis maximum of 92 rather than by the height of the axis gives 0.022, which is the honest figure and the one the picture does not show.
questions.hint: The plotted height is the distance from the bottom of the axis to the top, not the maximum value on it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why a reference without a persistent identifier is a gap
questions.learningObjective: explain what a reader loses when a reference cannot be resolved to the source
questions.stem: A reference list entry gives authors, title, journal and year but no persistent identifier, and the journal has since been reorganised so that a volume number no longer resolves. Explain what a reader trying to check the citation now faces, and what a persistent identifier is for.

answer.exemplar: The reader is reduced to searching, and searching is a different activity from checking. A persistent identifier is a string that resolves to the specific item rather than to a description of it, so a reader who has one can go straight to the version of record and see the passage the sentence rests on, whatever has happened to the journal's website, its volume numbering or the search engine's ranking since publication. Without it, the reader must reconstruct a query from the bibliographic description, and every step of that reconstruction is a place where the wrong paper can be substituted, because titles are not unique, reprints exist under several identifiers, and a paper that was later retracted or corrected still appears in the list exactly as it did before. That is the difference that matters: the failure mode is not inconvenience but silent misattribution, where a sentence carries a citation that appears to support it and does not. The honest claim to make about a source is that the reader can arrive at it, and an identifier is what makes that claim checkable rather than a matter of good intentions, which is why its absence is a substantive gap and not a formatting preference.

questions.explanation: A strong response distinguishes checking from searching, explains that a persistent identifier resolves to the specific item, and connects the absence of one to the risk of a citation pointing at the wrong paper.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader must do if the description they hold no longer resolves.

questions.topic: A sensitivity analysis kept out of sight
questions.learningObjective: explain why relegating a sensitivity analysis hides the finding that matters
questions.stem: A paper's results report one estimate, and a sensitivity analysis in the appendix shows that the estimate changes sign under a defensible alternative specification. Explain why this is more than a placement problem, and what a reader needs in order to weigh the result.

answer.exemplar: A sensitivity analysis is the part of a paper that reports what the estimate depends on, and a result whose direction is decided by a modelling choice the authors themselves consider defensible is not a settled finding that happened to need a technical appendix, it is a finding whose status is genuinely open. Putting it in the appendix leaves the main text asserting one number as though the choice behind it were settled, and readers who stop at the results, which is most of them including every systematic reviewer working to a deadline, never learn that the sign was in play. So the placement hides a fact about the strength of the evidence, which is why it is a reporting defect and not a matter of tidiness. What a reader needs is the alternative specification written out in enough detail to be re-run, the estimate it produces, and some statement of which specification the authors prefer and why, because a sensitivity analysis that lists twenty variations and concludes that they mostly agree has told the reader nothing about the one that matters. The honest arrangement puts the dependence in the results section, where it can be read alongside the estimate it qualifies, and leaves the full set of variations for the appendix to document.

questions.explanation: A strong response says a sign change under a defensible specification makes the result unsettled rather than merely technical, and identifies the specification, the alternative estimate and the authors' preference as what a reader needs.
questions.hint: Ask whether the main text would read the same to someone who never opens the appendix.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What an interval adds that a p value does not
questions.learningObjective: explain why an effect size with an interval answers a question a p value cannot
questions.stem: One paper reports a difference as statistically significant at the five per cent level with no effect size, and another reports an effect of 0.40 with an interval from 0.16 to 0.64. Explain what the second report lets a reader do that the first does not.

answer.exemplar: The first report is a yes-and-no answer wearing a number's clothes. It tells the reader that a result of this size or larger would have been unlikely, and nothing at all about how large the result actually was, so a difference of 0.02 and a difference of 1.20 pass the same test on the same data, and a reader cannot tell from the report which one occurred or whether either would matter to anybody. The second report supplies a magnitude and the range of magnitudes the data leave open, and the range is what turns the number into something a decision can use: a reader can see that the true effect is somewhere between small and moderate, that it is very unlikely to be zero, and that the study is too small to rule out an effect too small to act on. That last comparison is the one significance cannot make at all, because significance only tells a reader whether to reject a null and never how the estimate compares with a threshold that matters in practice. The interval also carries its own honesty about the study's precision, so two reports with the same central figure can be compared for how much they actually established, and a reader can tell a well-measured null from an underpowered one. The trap is treating the absence of an effect size as a stylistic shortfall rather than as the loss of the only part of the result that was ever in a position to matter.

questions.explanation: A strong response says significance is a yes-and-no answer that carries no magnitude, and identifies the interval's magnitude, its range and its comparison against a practical threshold as what it makes possible.
questions.hint: Ask whether a very small difference and a very large one would produce the same sentence.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a replication establishes
questions.learningObjective: explain why reproducing a result and reproducing its size are different achievements
questions.stem: A replication finds the same direction and a clear result, but an effect roughly half the size of the original. Explain why this is not a failed replication, and what the pair of findings has established between them.

answer.exemplar: A replication is not a request that a number come out identical, because the original number was one estimate from one sample of one size in one set of circumstances, and a second study that produces a clear result of the same direction has established the thing a replication exists to establish, which is that the effect is not an artefact of the first sample. It has also established something the original could not, which is a rough sense of the size, because two studies disagreeing about magnitude and agreeing about existence is the ordinary situation and the disagreement is information about how variable the estimate is rather than about whether there is anything there. A halving is unremarkable when the second study is smaller or noisier, since a noisier estimate wanders further from the truth in both directions and a single smaller study can easily land at half, and it is unremarkable in the other direction too when the second is better powered, in which case the smaller figure may be the more accurate one and the original the inflated one. What a replications of this kind genuinely cannot do is declare the original wrong, since no single smaller study can, and what it can do is put the original on record as an estimate whose precision nobody had characterised, which is the precondition for any future comparison of magnitudes to mean anything.

questions.explanation: A strong response says direction and existence are what a replication tests, that disagreement about magnitude is ordinary and informative, and that no single replication can declare the original wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what a replication is testing and what it is not.

answer.exemplar: Both displays are honest sentences and misleading pictures, and the reason is that a display carries two things at once, the numbers themselves and the frame in which they are read, and a reader attends to the first and is influenced by the second. The table's two means are correct and the omission is not a falsehood, but two means with no spread cannot be distinguished from one another however far apart they are, so the table cannot tell a reader whether the groups are two clouds that barely overlap or two clouds with no overlap at all, and a table that reports only a mean is a table that has quietly assumed the case is settled. The figure's bars are at the right heights and the axis is correctly labelled, and yet the axis spans four units while the difference spans two, so the gap fills half the plotted height for a change of about one part in forty-five, and the reader's eye reports a large multiple. What links the two is that neither can be caught by checking for untrue statements, which is why the discipline that catches them is a checklist about what is missing and what the frame is, applied by someone who has not written the sentence. Both also have honest versions that cost nothing: the spread beside the mean, and the axis starting at zero.

questions.explanation: A strong response treats omission and scaling as two ways a display misleads while stating nothing untrue, and notes that neither is caught by checking the prose for falsehoods.

questions.topic: What a conclusion may do and may not do

answer.exemplar: A conclusion is allowed to say more than the results section, and what it is allowed to say is more because it is interpretation rather than measurement. It may take a measured finding and say what it implies, so that a study showing a shorter average stay may properly conclude that the service is likely to be able to see more patients through the same beds, because that is a claim about what the numbers mean for the service and not a new observation. It may generalise within limits and say who else the finding probably holds for, provided it names the boundary of the population. What it may not do is introduce a fact, and persistence at twelve months is a fact of the same kind as the three-month measurement, since it says what is true about the world rather than what a true measurement implies, and it rests on nothing the study observed. The reason the distinction matters is that a conclusion is the part of a paper read on its own, so a new fact placed there is picked up by summaries, guidelines and later citations and travels without the three-month limit that would have made it honest. The two sentences look equally assertive, and the test that separates them is whether a reader could have been told they were wrong by anything in the paper, and a persistence claim could not.

questions.explanation: A strong response says a conclusion may interpret and generalise within named limits, that a claim about what will be true later is a new fact rather than an implication, and gives the test of whether the paper could have falsified it.

The magnitude and its interval follow, because a claim without a size is not actionable and attaching them shows how much is being asserted. The population and the limits of the sample are named before the rewriting, since they determine what the surviving claim may cover, and a claim is repaired within the boundaries of the evidence rather than by softening its verbs alone. Only then is the sentence rewritten and the remainder deleted, which is the step that is hardest to do and the one that makes the difference between a paper that has been checked and one that has been made agreeable.
questions.hint: Specify the claim before deciding how much of it survives.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A rate reported with the wrong population beneath it
questions.learningObjective: interpret a reported rate whose denominator does not match the group at risk
questions.stem: A report gives 12 readmissions within thirty days across 4,200 procedures and states that readmissions run at 12 per 4,200 people treated. What is the fair reading?

options.text: The count and its base are both given and the division is right, but the phrase people treated is not, because the events are counted per procedure and some people had more than one
The report is accurate throughout, since procedures and people are the same units in a service that treats one patient per procedure
options.misconception: assumes a one-to-one relation between procedures and people

options.text: The rate is understated, because the correct base for readmissions is all patients rather than all procedures
options.misconception: proposes a different base without establishing that the current one is wrong

options.text: The figure cannot be checked, because thirty days of follow-up is too short a window for any readmission rate to mean anything
options.misconception: rejects a stated definition of the window rather than checking the base

questions.explanation: The arithmetic in the report is sound and the base is stated, and the problem is one word deep, since a count of events divided by a count of procedures is a rate per procedure and calling it a rate per person treated quietly assumes each person contributed one procedure, which is false wherever anyone was readmitted more than once or had two procedures in the period. Option B is the assumption that makes the phrasing seem harmless. Option C offers a competing base without showing that procedures is the wrong one, and a rate per procedure is a legitimate quantity when the event is attached to the procedure. Option D dismisses a stated follow-up window rather than examining the denominator.
questions.hint: Ask whether one person can appear more than once in the count of procedures.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A replication pair read together
questions.learningObjective: interpret two studies whose centres differ and whose intervals overlap
questions.stem: An original study reports 0.40 with an interval from 0.10 to 0.70. A replication reports 0.05 with an interval from minus 0.25 to 0.35. The replication is described as having failed to reproduce the finding. What is the fair reading?

options.text: The two intervals share a region, so the studies are not describing incompatible effects, and the disagreement is about size rather than about whether there is anything there
The replication failed, because its central estimate is close to zero and a central estimate is what a finding consists of
options.misconception: judges a study by its centre while ignoring the range around it

options.text: The original is in doubt, because a second study that disagrees is by definition better informed than the first
options.misconception: treats any disagreement as evidence against whichever study came first

options.text: Neither can be assessed, because two studies that disagree cannot both be reported and a paper may only describe one of them
options.misconception: treats a divergence as a reason to suppress one of the studies

questions.explanation: The ranges overlap from 0.10 to 0.35, so there is a stretch of effect size that both sets of data are compatible with, and two studies that share such a stretch are not contradicting each other however far apart their central figures sit, which means the disagreement is a disagreement about magnitude and not about existence. The replication has therefore told us the direction is compatible with a small effect and possibly with none, and told us the original's estimate is less precise than its width suggested, which is what makes any future comparison of magnitudes worth attempting. Option B is the failure of attention the interval exists to prevent. Option C decides disputes by seniority of publication. Option D is the wrong conclusion to draw, since a divergence between two studies is reportable information rather than a reason to publish one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two ranges share any ground.
